Red-breasted parakeets (Psittacula alexandri) incubate their eggs for approximately 28 days [ab = approximately 28 days] when maintained at a temperature of 33 °C [T = 33 °C], a duration that aligns closely with the incubation periods documented for other medium-sized Asian parrots. Newly hatched chicks emerge at a wet weight of about 9.3 grams [Ww0 = about 9.3 grams], a value derived from the typical egg dimensions of this species, which range from 29 to 31.9 millimeters in length and 24.1 to 24.6 millimeters in width. This initial mass is modest and reflects the altricial condition of psittacine neonates, which rely entirely on parental provisioning during the initial days post-hatching. The eggshell itself is a calcareous structure providing essential physical protection, while the albumen-buffered embryo develops over the incubation period. The 9.3 gram hatchling mass is substantially lower than that of comparably sized precocial birds, underscoring the altricial strategy of investing in rapid postnatal growth rather than large initial yolk reserves.

In terms of mass, adult females of the Red-breasted parakeet attain an ultimate wet weight of 147 grams [Wwi = 147 grams], a figure that falls within the reported range of 133 to 168 grams for this species. This adult mass is consistent with the general body size of Psittacula members, which are medium-sized parakeets with robust bodies and long, graduated tails. The 147 gram value represents a substantial increase from the 9.3 gram hatchling mass, reflecting a period of rapid somatic growth during the nestling and fledgling phases. Male adults are broadly comparable in size, though females sometimes exhibit a slightly lower body mass. The energetic costs of reaching this adult mass are considerable, requiring efficient food intake and digestion to support the rapid development of feathers, musculature, and skeletal structures. Individual variation in ultimate body mass is influenced by local food availability, habitat quality, and seasonal fluctuations in fruit and seed abundance.

This energetic measurement provides insight into the species' metabolic demands, which are shaped by its frugivorous and granivorous diet and its active, arboreal lifestyle within tropical and subtropical forests. The value is relatively high for a bird of its body mass, possibly reflecting the energetic expenses associated with flight and social behaviours in a species that lives in flocks. The 41.3 °C body temperature is a standard avian endothermic condition, and the oxygen consumption at this temperature serves as a benchmark for comparing metabolic rates across the Psittacidae family. Field studies have confirmed that this metabolic rate is sufficient to support the daily energetic costs of foraging, territory defense, and reproductive activities.

Within the same thermal regime of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], the species exhibits a maximum reproductive rate expressed through a clutch size of 3 to 4 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 3 to 4 eggs per clutch] and a single clutch produced each year [F_R_i = single clutch produced each year]. This annual reproductive output is typical for many Psittacula species, which invest considerable parental care into a relatively small number of offspring each breeding season. The decision to produce only one clutch per year is likely influenced by the extended period of dependency that nestlings require, as well as the seasonal availability of key food resources such as figs, fruits, and seeds. Nestlings remain in the nest for a considerable period before achieving nutritional independence, and the limited clutch frequency reflects the high per-offspring investment. Comparing this species to other parrots of similar body size, the annual reproductive rate is consistent with life history strategies that favor quality over quantity in offspring production.

In contrast, the attainment of sexual maturity is reached at 150 days after hatching [tp = 150 days after hatching], a relatively rapid maturation compared to larger psittacines at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C].
